title: Tonkatsu
description: Thick pork loin cutlets breaded in panko and double-fried until the crust shatters, served sliced over shredded cabbage with tangy tonkatsu sauce.

ingredients.item: boneless pork loin cutlets, about 120g each

ingredients.note: bottled, or mix ketchup, Worcestershire and oyster sauce

steps: Trim excess fat from the pork loin cutlets and snip the connective tissue at the edges in 3-4 spots so they do not curl while frying.
Pound each cutlet lightly with the back of a knife, then season both sides with salt and pepper.
Set up a breading station: flour, then beaten egg, then panko, and coat each cutlet in that order, pressing the panko on firmly.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to 170C (a panko crumb dropped in should sizzle and float within a few seconds).
Fry the cutlets for 3-4 minutes per side until golden brown, then rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes so the crust stays crisp.
Slice each cutlet crosswise into strips and fan them back into shape on top of the shredded cabbage.
Serve with tonkatsu sauce drizzled over or on the side, and a bowl of steamed rice and miso soup.
tips: Keep the oil at 170C by frying only two cutlets at a time; overcrowding drops the temperature and makes the crust greasy.
Resting the fried cutlets on a rack instead of paper towels keeps the underside from steaming soft.
nutritionNote: Deep-fried and protein-rich; balance the plate with the shredded cabbage and a light miso soup rather than extra fried sides.

title: Sukiyaki
description: Thinly sliced beef and vegetables simmered tableside in a sweet-savory soy and mirin broth, each bite dipped in raw beaten egg before eating.

ingredients.item: thinly sliced beef ribeye or chuck
ingredients.note: ask the butcher for shabu-shabu cut

ingredients.item: napa cabbage, cut into wide strips
negi or leek, sliced on a diagonal

ingredients.note: raw; omit or use pasteurised egg for young kids

steps: Combine the soy sauce, mirin, sugar and water or dashi in a small pot and warm until the sugar dissolves; this is the warishita sauce.
Arrange the beef, cabbage, shungiku, shirataki, mushrooms, negi and tofu on a large platter.
Heat a shallow cast-iron or electric skillet at the table and add a thin layer of the warishita sauce.
Sear a few slices of beef first until just browned, pushing them to one side of the pan.
Add the vegetables, tofu and shirataki in batches, spooning warishita over them and simmering until just tender.
Crack an egg into each diner's small bowl and beat lightly; dip each cooked piece into the egg before eating.
Top up the pan with more warishita sauce and ingredients as it empties, keeping the broth simmering gently throughout the meal.
tips: Do not let the broth boil hard once the vegetables release water, or it turns overly salty as it reduces; add a splash of water to balance.
kidNote: Serve the kids' beef and vegetables cooked through and skip the raw-egg dip for them, offering a little extra warishita spooned over rice instead.
nutritionNote: Rich in protein and iron from the beef; balance the sodium from soy and mirin with the leafy greens and tofu already in the pot rather than added salt.

title: Buta no Kakuni
description: Pork belly braised low and slow in soy, sake, mirin and sugar until fork-tender and glossy, a Nagasaki home-cooking classic served over rice.

ingredients.item: pork belly block, skin on or off

ingredients.note: optional, to simmer in at the end

steps: Cut the pork belly into large 4cm cubes and place in a pot with water, ginger slices and green onion tops.
Bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered for 45 minutes, skimming off scum, until the pork is tender.
Drain the pork and rinse off any scum clinging to the surface; discard the parboiling liquid.
Return the pork to a clean pot with fresh dashi, soy sauce, sake, mirin, sugar and ginger, adding water to just cover.
Cover with a drop lid (or parchment paper pressed onto the surface) and simmer gently for 45-60 minutes until very tender.
Add the soft-boiled eggs for the last 15 minutes so they absorb the sauce without turning rubbery.
Uncover and simmer a further 10 minutes to reduce the sauce to a glossy glaze, spooning it over the pork as it thickens.
Serve the pork and eggs over rice with the reduced sauce spooned on top and sliced green onion scattered over.
tips: The parboil-and-rinse step removes the strong porky smell; do not skip it.
Kakuni tastes even better the next day once the fat has had time to firm up and the flavour has settled; refrigerate and reheat gently.
nutritionNote: High in fat from the pork belly; serve smaller portions alongside plain rice and a vinegary or bitter vegetable side like sunomono to cut the richness.

title: Omurice
description: Ketchup-fried chicken rice wrapped in a soft, thin omelette, a yoshoku diner favourite that kids know from anime lunchboxes as much as home kitchens.
steps: Melt the butter in a large pan over medium heat and saute the onion until translucent.
Add the diced chicken and cook until no longer pink, about 4 minutes.
Stir in the rice, breaking up clumps, then add ketchup and soy sauce and toss until every grain is coated; season with salt and pepper and set aside, keeping warm.
Whisk 2 eggs with 1 tablespoon of milk per portion until fully combined.
Melt a little butter in a small nonstick pan over medium-low heat, pour in the egg mixture and swirl to coat the pan in a thin layer.
Cook until just set but still slightly runny on top, then spoon a quarter of the ketchup rice into the centre in an oval mound.
Fold the omelette edges over the rice using a spatula, then invert the pan over a plate so the omelette lands seam-side down.
Repeat for the remaining portions and finish each with a squeeze of ketchup on top.
tips: Using day-old rice keeps the fried rice from turning mushy when the ketchup is added.
If the omelette tears, just patch it with a spare thin egg sheet before flipping it over the rice.
nutritionNote: A balanced one-bowl meal of protein, egg and carbohydrate; add a side salad or vegetable soup since the dish itself is light on vegetables.

title: Hamburg Steak
description: A juicy pan-seared patty of ground beef and pork bound with panko and onion, finished with a glossy soy-ketchup demi-glace, Japan's favourite yoshoku comfort food.

ingredients.note: or use water to keep it alcohol-free

steps: Melt the butter in a pan and cook the minced onion over low heat until soft and sweet, about 8 minutes; cool to room temperature.
Soak the panko in milk in a large bowl until absorbed.
Add the ground beef, pork, cooled onion, egg, salt, pepper and nutmeg to the bowl and mix with your hands until sticky and well combined.
Divide into 4 portions and shape into oval patties, tossing each between your palms to knock out air pockets, then dent the centre slightly.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium-high heat and sear the patties for 2 minutes per side until browned.
Lower the heat, cover, and cook for 8-10 minutes, flipping once, until the juices run clear and the centre is no longer pink.
Remove the patties, then add ketchup, Worcestershire sauce, soy sauce and wine or water to the same pan, scraping up the browned bits.
Simmer the sauce for 2 minutes until slightly thickened, swirl in the butter, and spoon over the patties to serve.
tips: Cooling the sauteed onion before mixing keeps the raw meat from warming up and losing its bind.
Cook a tiny test patty first to check the seasoning before shaping the rest.
nutritionNote: A good source of iron and protein; pair with steamed vegetables or a side salad to offset the richness of the meat and butter sauce.

title: Korokke
description: Mashed potato and sauteed ground meat formed into patties, breaded in panko and deep-fried to a crisp golden shell, a butcher-shop and home-kitchen staple.
steps: Boil the potatoes in salted water until a fork slides through easily, about 12 minutes, then drain and mash while still hot.
Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a pan and saute the onion until soft, then add the ground beef and cook until browned, breaking it apart.
Season the meat with soy sauce, sugar, salt and pepper, then fold it into the mashed potato until evenly combined.
Cool the mixture until easy to handle, then shape into 8 oval patties about 2cm thick.
Coat each patty in flour, then beaten egg, then panko, pressing the crumbs on firmly.
Heat the deep-frying oil to 180C and fry the patties in batches for 2-3 minutes, turning once, until deep golden brown.
Drain on a wire rack for a minute before serving with tonkatsu sauce or ketchup and a wedge of cabbage.
tips: Mash the potatoes while hot for a smoother texture, and let the filling cool fully before breading or the panko will not stick.
Shaped, uncooked korokke freeze well for a month; fry straight from frozen, adding 2 extra minutes.
nutritionNote: Starchy and fried, so it is filling on its own; serve with a vegetable side or salad rather than another starch to round out the plate.

title: Oden
description: A gentle simmer of fish cakes, daikon, eggs, konnyaku and tofu in clear soy-dashi broth, the classic winter hot pot sold from street stalls and made at home alike.

ingredients.item: konnyaku, scored and cut into triangles

steps: Peel the daikon rounds and bevel the edges slightly so they hold their shape; boil in plain water for 15 minutes to soften and remove bitterness, then drain.
Score the konnyaku pieces in a crosshatch pattern and parboil for 2 minutes to remove any strong smell; drain.
Combine the dashi, soy sauce, mirin and salt in a large pot and bring to a gentle simmer.
Add the daikon, eggs, konnyaku and atsuage first, since they need the longest to absorb flavour, and simmer uncovered for 30 minutes on low heat.
Add the fish cakes and simmer a further 10-15 minutes, keeping the broth at a gentle simmer and never a rolling boil, or it turns cloudy.
Turn off the heat and let everything sit in the broth for at least 20 minutes before serving so the flavour deepens further.
Ladle into bowls with plenty of broth and serve with a small dab of karashi mustard on the side for the adults.
tips: Oden tastes better the next day; make it ahead and reheat gently without boiling.
Keep the broth at a bare simmer throughout — boiling breaks up the fish cakes and clouds the broth.
kidNote: Leave the karashi mustard off the kids' bowls entirely and serve it only on the side for adults, since it is sharply hot.
nutritionNote: The broth and fish cakes carry a fair amount of sodium; go light on extra soy sauce at the table and pair with plain rice to balance the meal.

title: Buri Daikon
description: Yellowtail simmered with daikon in a sweet soy and sake broth until the fish is glazed and the daikon has soaked up all the flavour, a wintertime izakaya and home favourite.

ingredients.note: skin on, from a Japanese or seafood grocer

ingredients.item: daikon, peeled and cut into thick rounds
ginger knob, sliced into thin rounds

steps: Salt the yellowtail pieces on both sides and let sit for 15 minutes to draw out excess moisture and fishy smell, then pat dry.
Bring a pot of water to a boil and blanch the fish for 30 seconds per side until the surface just turns white; transfer to iced water, then rinse away any scum and pat dry.
Boil the daikon rounds in fresh water for 15 minutes until a skewer slides in with slight resistance, then drain.
In a wide pot, combine 2 cups water, ginger, sugar, sake and mirin and bring to a simmer.
Add the daikon first and simmer for 10 minutes so it absorbs the broth before the delicate fish goes in.
Add the soy sauce and the blanched yellowtail, cover with a drop lid or parchment, and simmer gently for 12-15 minutes, spooning broth over occasionally.
Remove the drop lid for the last few minutes and let the sauce reduce slightly until glossy.
Serve the fish and daikon together with a little broth spooned over, garnished with sliced green onion.
tips: The salt-and-blanch step is what keeps this dish from tasting fishy — do not skip it.
The daikon actually improves overnight in the fridge as it keeps absorbing the broth; reheat gently before serving.
kidNote: Debone the yellowtail collar carefully before serving to the kids, as it has small bones near the fin.
nutritionNote: Yellowtail is rich in omega-3 fats; the broth is salty, so serve with plain rice and a small side of blanched greens to round out the meal.

title: Chikuzenni
description: Chicken and root vegetables such as lotus root, carrot, burdock and konjac simmered together in a sweet soy dashi, a New Year and everyday nimono from Kyushu.

ingredients.item: boneless chicken thigh, cut into bite-size pieces
carrot, peeled and cut into rolling wedges
lotus root, peeled and cut into half-moons
burdock root (gobo), scrubbed and cut on a diagonal
ingredients.note: or use extra carrot and mushroom

ingredients.item: konnyaku, scored and torn into pieces
dried shiitake mushrooms, rehydrated and halved
dashi or reserved shiitake soaking liquid

steps: Heat the oil in a large pot and stir-fry the chicken pieces until lightly browned on the outside.
Add the carrot, lotus root, burdock and konnyaku and stir-fry for 2-3 minutes until coated in the chicken fat.
Add the shiitake mushrooms, then pour in the dashi or shiitake soaking liquid, soy sauce, sugar, mirin and sake.
Bring to a boil, skim off any scum, then cover with a drop lid and simmer on medium-low heat for 20 minutes.
Remove the drop lid and continue simmering for 10-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the liquid has mostly reduced and coats the vegetables.
Taste and adjust with a little more soy sauce if needed, then turn off the heat and let sit for 10 minutes so the flavour settles.
Serve warm or at room temperature, topped with the blanched snow peas for a spot of green.
tips: Cutting the root vegetables into similar-sized rolling wedges (rangiri) helps them cook evenly and look traditional.
This dish keeps well for 3-4 days refrigerated and tastes even better the next day.
nutritionNote: A fibre-rich vegetable and lean protein dish; the soy-mirin broth is salty, so serve with plain rice rather than extra soy sauce at the table.

title: Takikomi Gohan
description: Short-grain rice cooked in one pot with dashi, soy sauce, chicken and mushrooms so every grain soaks up savoury flavour, a simple everyday rice-cooker dinner.

ingredients.item: aburaage fried tofu pouch, thinly sliced

steps: Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear, then drain well in a sieve for 15 minutes.
Combine the dashi, soy sauce, mirin, sake and a pinch of salt in a measuring cup and stir to dissolve.
Place the drained rice in a rice cooker or heavy pot and pour the seasoned dashi over it, leveling the rice but not stirring.
Scatter the chicken, shiitake, carrot and aburaage evenly over the top of the rice without mixing them in.
Start the rice cooker on the regular setting, or cover the pot and cook on the stovetop: bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest heat for 12-13 minutes.
Once cooking finishes, let the rice rest covered for 10 minutes without opening the lid.
Fluff gently with a rice paddle, folding the toppings through the rice from the bottom up, then garnish with green onion before serving.
tips: Do not stir the ingredients into the rice before cooking — layering them on top keeps the rice from turning gummy.
The unattended rice-cooker or resting time is not counted in the active cook time above; budget an extra 20-30 minutes if using a standard rice cooker cycle.
nutritionNote: A balanced one-pot meal of rice, lean chicken and vegetables; go light on extra soy sauce at the table since the rice is already seasoned.
